entities.summary:
Pepi II Neferkare was a king of the Sixth Dynasty in Egypt's Old Kingdom, ruling from 2281 to 2180 BCE. He succeeded to the throne at age six, after the death of Nemtyemsaf I, and reigned for 90 years, the longest reign in Egyptian history at that time.

As a child pharaoh, Pepi II faced numerous challenges, including conflicts with neighboring kingdoms and internal power struggles within his own court. Despite these obstacles, he managed to maintain Egypt's position as a major power in the region, and his reign is often referred to as the 'Golden Age' of the Old Kingdom.

Pepi II's legacy extends beyond his own reign, as he laid the groundwork for the development of ancient Egyptian literature, art, and architecture. His reign saw the construction of numerous temples, tombs, and monuments, including the famous Step Pyramid at Saqqara, which became a symbol of ancient Egyptian engineering and architectural ingenuity.

The exact circumstances of Pepi II's death are still debated among historians, with some attributing it to a natural illness, while others propose that he may have been assassinated. Regardless, his impact on Egyptian history and culture is undeniable, and he remains one of the most fascinating and enigmatic figures of the ancient world.

The discovery of a previously unknown tomb near the Step Pyramid has shed new light on Pepi II's life and reign, revealing a complex and multifaceted individual who defied the conventional wisdom of child pharaohs. This latest archaeological find has sparked renewed interest in the life and legacy of Pepi II, and promises to continue rewriting the narrative of ancient Egyptian history for years to come.
